abstract: This review article synthesizes research on affective polarization in the United States—the growing tendency of Democrats and Republicans to dislike, distrust, and avoid one another as social groups rather than merely disagreeing over policy. It distinguishes this affective, identity-based form of division from traditional issue-based polarization and examines its origins, measurement, and downstream effects. The authors argue that partisan animosity has become a defining feature of contemporary American mass politics.
key_claims: A new form of polarization—affective polarization—has emerged in the American mass public, distinct from issue-based or ideological polarization.
Partisans increasingly view members of the opposing party negatively, attributing traits such as hypocrisy, selfishness, and closed-mindedness to them.
This animosity extends beyond politics into social life, with partisans unwilling to socialize or associate across party lines.
Affective polarization is rooted in partisanship functioning as a social identity that triggers in-group favoritism and out-group hostility.
methods: Literature review and synthesis of existing empirical research on partisan affect and polarization
Draws on the theoretical framework of social identity theory to interpret partisan attitudes
Traces the origins and consequences of affective polarization across prior studies (specific datasets not detailed in the abstract)
findings: Partisans express strong dislike and distrust toward out-party members.
Negative stereotypes (hypocritical, selfish, closed-minded) are commonly ascribed to the opposing party.
Partisan animosity manifests as social distance, including reluctance to interact or socialize across party lines.
contributions: Consolidates and frames the concept of affective polarization as a distinct object of study within political science.
Provides an integrative account of the origins and consequences of interparty animosity in the mass public.
Positions social identity as a central explanatory mechanism for contemporary partisan hostility.
framing: The paper situates itself within the study of American political behavior and partisanship, reframing polarization away from purely ideological or issue-based conflict toward an affective, social-identity-based understanding of division between Democrats and Republicans.
